summary: Bangladesh lies in the delta of the Ganges and Brahmaputra rivers in South Asia, is one of the most densely populated countries in the world, and became independent from Pakistan in 1971.

ranking.name: Islam (mainly Sunni)
ranking.description: Islam entered in the early 13th century when the Turkic Muslim army led by Bakhtiyar Khalji conquered Bengal in 1204, after which Sufi saints cleared forests and founded villages in the eastern Bengal delta, attracting large numbers of farmers to convert. At the partition of India and Pakistan in 1947, East Bengal, with its Muslim majority, was assigned to Pakistan, and it became independent as Bangladesh in 1971; Muslims make up about nine tenths.

ranking.name: Hinduism
ranking.description: Hinduism was once one of the main religions of Bengal, but the 1947 partition, the religious riots of 1950 and 1964, and the massacres of Hindus by the Pakistani army during the 1971 war of independence sent millions of Hindus fleeing to West Bengal in India. The share of Hindus has fallen from about three tenths in 1901 to about 8 percent today, found mainly in Khulna, Dhaka and Sylhet.

ranking.name: Buddhism
ranking.description: Buddhism has a long history in Bengal; the Pala dynasty of the 8th to 12th centuries was an important Buddhist dynasty and built the Somapura Mahavihara at Paharpur (now a World Heritage Site). Buddhism declined with the Hindu Sena dynasty of the 12th century and the Islamic conquest of the 13th century, and today Buddhists are mainly peoples such as the Chakma and Marma of the Chittagong Hill Tracts in the southeast, making up about 1 percent.

religion.background: In ancient times the Bengal region was an important center of Buddhism and Hinduism; the Pala dynasty of the 8th to 12th centuries supported Buddhism, while the Sena dynasty promoted Hinduism. After the Turkic Muslim conquest of Bengal in 1204, Islam expanded in the eastern delta with Sufi saints and agricultural clearance, and during the Mughal Empire of the 16th to 18th centuries the Muslim population of East Bengal increased greatly. After the 1947 partition East Bengal became East Pakistan, and it became independent in 1971; the 1972 constitution had secularism as a basic principle, and the 1988 amendment made Islam the state religion, while still guaranteeing other religions.

language.official: Bengali is the only official language.

ranking.name: Bengali
ranking.description: Bengali derives from the Prakrits of ancient India, took shape around the 10th century, and from the 14th century gradually developed a literary tradition. In 1948 the Pakistani government declared Urdu the sole national language, provoking the language movement in East Pakistan; on 21 February 1952 student demonstrators at the University of Dhaka were fired on by police and soldiers and several were killed. This movement ultimately led to Bangladesh's independence in 1971, and UNESCO designated 21 February 'International Mother Language Day'. Today about 98 percent of the population speak Bengali as a mother tongue.

ranking.name: Other minority languages (Chakma, etc.)
ranking.description: The minority languages of Bangladesh are found mainly in the Chittagong Hill Tracts in the southeast and in the northeast, and include Chakma and Marma (of the Burmese group) as well as Garo, Santali and others. These peoples have long been under pressure from the mainstream Bengali culture, armed conflict broke out in the Chittagong Hill Tracts in the 1970s to 1990s, and mother-tongue education has been promoted only gradually since the 1997 peace accord.

language.history: Bengali is an Indo-Aryan language that developed from the Eastern Prakrits around the 10th century, and its earliest literary work is the Charyapada of Buddhist monks. In the medieval period under Islamic rule Bengali absorbed a great deal of Persian and Arabic vocabulary; in the Bengali Renaissance of the 19th century the poet Tagore made Bengali literature famous around the world and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913. The language movement of 1952 was the starting point of Bengali nationalism, and after independence in 1971 Bengali became the sole official language.

ranking.name: Shorshe Ilish
ranking.description: Hilsa fish is cut into pieces and steamed or stewed with mustard paste, mustard oil, turmeric and green chilies; it is pungent and nose-tingling and is eaten with plain rice.
ranking.history: The hilsa is the national fish of Bangladesh; every rainy season it swims upstream from the Bay of Bengal into the Ganges and Meghna rivers to spawn, and delta fishermen have made a living catching hilsa for hundreds of years. Mustard oil and mustard paste are distinctive seasonings of Bengali cooking, clearly different from North Indian cuisine. Hilsa is indispensable at the festive meals of the Bengali New Year (around 14 April) and is also a shared cultural symbol of Bangladesh and the Indian state of West Bengal.

ranking.name: Biryani
ranking.description: Basmati rice is layered with lamb or beef and potatoes and cooked in a sealed pot with saffron, ghee and spices; the grains stay separate and the aroma is rich.
ranking.history: Biryani derives from the Persian pilaf and came to South Asia with the Mughal court in the 16th to 18th centuries; Dhaka, as the capital of Mughal Bengal (from 1610), developed its own style. The 'Kacchi Biryani' of Old Dhaka (raw marinated meat cooked together with the rice) is the most famous, and the versions of the old-established restaurants of Old Dhaka are the signature the locals are proud of. It is an indispensable festive dish at weddings, Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha.

ranking.name: Panta Bhat
ranking.description: Leftover rice is soaked in water overnight so that it ferments slightly and turns sour, and the next day it is eaten with green chilies, onion, salt and fried fish or pickles, cool and refreshing in hot weather.
ranking.history: Panta bhat is a traditional breakfast of Bengali farmers; in the days without refrigerators, soaking in water and fermenting kept leftover rice from spoiling, and the fermented rice is cooling in hot weather. In recent years it has been tied to the Bengali New Year (Pohela Boishakh), when city dwellers eat panta bhat with fried hilsa on the morning of 14 April, symbolizing a return to village tradition.

ranking.name: Pitha
ranking.description: Various steamed, pan-fried and fried cakes made mainly from rice flour with coconut, palm sugar or date sugar, in dozens of shapes and flavors.
ranking.history: Pitha are traditional winter sweets of Bangladesh, closely tied to the rice harvest. Every year in late autumn and early winter, when the new rice is harvested, villages hold 'Nabanna' (the new rice festival) and grind the new rice into flour to make pitha in celebration. The date sugar (khejur gur) made by boiling down date palm sap harvested in winter is an important source of sweetness, so winter is called the 'pitha season', and cities also hold pitha festivals.

ranking.name: Mishti Doi
ranking.description: Milk is sweetened and boiled down until slightly caramel-colored, then poured into clay pots and fermented into a sweet yogurt with a thick texture and a faint aroma of caramel and milk.
ranking.history: Mishti doi is one of the most popular sweets of the Bengal region, and the sweet yogurt of the northern city of Bogura is the most famous; it is said to have been made since the 19th century and became known across Bengal in the British colonial period. Serving it in clay pots absorbs excess moisture and makes the yogurt thicker. In Bengali culture sweets are given at happy occasions, weddings and festivals, and mishti doi is the indispensable final dessert at a banquet.
